Motivation & Key Observations LLM serving needs both fast access and economical capacity GPU HBM Fast access Limited capacity Host DRAM More capacity Higher latency SSD / disk Economical capacity Lower bandwidth Limited HBM Long contexts and concurrent requests need more KV-cache capacity. Static provisioning Fixed capacities can leave storage over- or under-provisioned. Workload diversity Reuse patterns and request density change the value of each tier. Source: Kareto v1, Abstract and §§1–2, pp. 1–2. Preprint; no venue claim. Main 02 / 16

Cache Capacity Saturation and Diminishing Returns Capacity adds reuse, but marginal gains fall after the working set is covered Capacity and reuse Cache capacity can grow without a proportional increase in reuse ratio. As capacity gets larger, the reuse gains gradually taper. More cache capacity helps, but reuse gains taper as the cache grows. TTL and lifetime Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.1.2, Figure 3, p. 4. Main 04 / 16

Workload Density Changes the Value of SSD Prefetching Kareto uses existing queue time as a prefetch window; it does not add queueing deliberately Compute-abundant / low density time short queue I/O wait GPU work SSD read Short queues cannot hide disk reads, so the request waits for I/O or recomputes. Compute-constrained / high density time existing queue GPU work SSD read ready before use Longer existing queues can hide more disk I/O and enable cache reuse. SSD caching helps when its data becomes ready before dependent GPU computation. Figures 5–6 Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.3, observations 1–4, pp. 5–6. Main 05 / 16

Density Changes Reuse, Throughput, and TTFT The same capacity increase affects service metrics differently across workload densities Metric Compute-Constrained (Low Density) Compute-Abundant (High Density) Reuse Ratio Increasing capacity usually raises reuse. Increasing capacity can also raise reuse. Throughput Less recomputation may improve throughput. Workload arrivals limit throughput gains. TTFT Less prefill and queueing can improve TTFT. Capacity mainly improves individual request latency. Workload density changes how capacity gains translate into performance. Figure 5 detail Figure 6 detail Original Figure 5, Kareto v1, Section 3.3, p. 5. Main 06 / 16

Kareto Optimizes Throughput, Latency, and Economic Cost The objectives define a Pareto set, not one universal optimum Multi-objective formulation minx∈X (E[L(x)], −E[T(x)], C(x)) Objective Optimization Direction Latency Lower is better Throughput Higher is better Economic Cost Lower is better Storage configurations The authors compare pure DRAM, pure disk, and hybrid configurations using 256 GB DRAM with different disk capacities. Hybrid storage can combine DRAM’s faster access with SSD’s lower capacity cost, offering different cost-performance trade-offs. Different service objectives favor different non-dominated storage configurations. Bandwidth sensitivity Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.1, Eqs. 1–2 and Figure 8, pp. 3–4, 7. Cost is economic expenditure, not energy. Main 07 / 16

Kareto Uses an End-to-End Discrete-Event Simulator The authors develop their own trace-driven simulator; it is not LLMServingSim KV Cache Simulator Tracks prefix-tree reuse and KV placement across DRAM and disk/SSD, including cache hits, insertions, and evictions. Request Metadata Replays timestamps, input length, cache-hit length, and decode length. Scheduler & Queue Models waiting and running requests, scheduling decisions, and batch formation. Performance Modeling Uses offline profiling samples to predict execution latency and cache-transfer time. Architecture detail Figure 4 and Section 3.2, p. 4. Figure 4 is displayed with original panels and labels. Main 08 / 16

Adaptive Pareto Search for Storage Configuration Simulation-driven configuration planning using historical workload traces Workload Traces Recent requests seed planning and replay. Parameter Planner Proposes DRAM-capacity and disk-TTL configurations. Group TTL Manager Assigns retention TTLs to reused prefix groups. Adaptive Searcher Prunes weak regions and refines valuable candidates. Performance Simulator Evaluates throughput, latency, and economic cost. Pareto Selector Keeps non-dominated configurations. Online Serving System Applies the selected configuration and tracks outcomes. System workflow Search ablation Original Figure 9. Kareto v1, Sections 4.1–4.2; Algorithm 1 and Section 5.3.1, Figure 13. Main 09 / 16

Group-Specific TTL Optimization under a Shared Storage Budget Different KV cache reuse patterns require different retention policies Workload-Aware Grouping Partition KV blocks into groups based on frequently reused prefix subtrees. Assign different TTLs according to each group’s reuse patterns. Allocate disk retention resources under a shared storage budget. 1. Per-Group TTL Selection ROIg(t) = Hg(t) Cg(t) Choose each group’s ROI-efficient TTL to maximize cache hits per unit of storage capacity-time. 2. Global TTL Optimization max t X g Hg(tg) s.t. X g Cg(tg) ≤B Adjust group TTLs to maximize total cache hits within the shared storage budget. Notation: Hg(t): cache hits; Cg(t): storage capacity-time consumption; B: total storage capacity-time budget. Group-specific TTLs maximize cache reuse under limited disk storage resources. Reuse groups ROI allocation Source: Kareto v1, Sections 4.1–4.3, Figures 9–11, Algorithms 1–2. Main 10 / 16

Evaluation Uses Three Trace Types and Two Cluster Scales The paper evaluates a Qwen3-480B / SGLang serving setup with ESSD PL1 Trace Workload A Interactive chatbot; derived from an open-source dataset. B Programmatic API with shared prompts; derived from an open-source dataset. C Synthetic agent workload reflecting internal request characteristics. Each two-hour trace contains 40k–170k requests. Trace C is synthetic; not all traces are production. System and scenarios Model: Qwen3-480B Serving engine: SGLang Storage: Alibaba Cloud ESSD PL1 Baseline: fixed 1,024 GB DRAM 1 instance: compute-constrained 4 instances: compute-abundant Instances are cloud compute instances, not GPU counts. The paper does not specify the accelerator model/count or parallelism used in the emulated evaluation. Workload provenance and compute scale shape how the reported outcomes should be read. Storage sensitivity Source: Kareto v1, Sections 3.3 and 5.1–5.2, pp. 5, 9–10. Main 11 / 16

Potential Research Directions and Research Gaps Research opportunities informed by Kareto and GreenCache Research Direction Potential Gap Research Opportunity Fine-Grained Energy Modeling Limited activity-aware energy modeling in the reviewed work. Model GPU operations, storage I/O, and data transfers. Energy-Aware Cache Configuration Performance- and cost-optimal configurations may not be energy-optimal. Fine-grained system energy modeling can support energy- and carbon-aware cache management. Accounting Details Proposed modeling scope informed by GreenCache and Carbon–SLO. Main 16 / 16

Backup B1 — KV Cache Lifetime and Storage Requirements Oracle TTL illustrates how reuse intervals affect active storage The paper’s oracle policy sets TTL to zero for blocks that will never be accessed again. Cumulative blocks continue to grow while active blocks remain much lower under this retrospective bound. Reuse concentration Capacity saturation Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.1, Figure 1. Oracle is an analysis reference, not an online-known future. B01

Backup B2 — DRAM Bandwidth Sensitivity Bandwidth constraints can dominate TTFT in the paper’s simulation table Large TTFT changes occur at low bandwidth; improvements taper at higher rates. Preserve units as reported. The table’s values are simulation outputs, not a universal hardware law. Density results Objectives Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.1, Table 1, p. 4. B02

Backup B3 — Disk Bandwidth and Capacity Are Coupled Writes from eviction and reads for reload share constrained I/O resources In this cloud-disk setting, bandwidth scales with provisioned capacity and read/write contention matters. Capacity beyond total KV footprint may still change effective performance. Density results Trade-offs Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.3, Figure 7, p. 6. B03

Backup B4 — Workload Density and Storage Capacity Full Figure 5 results for reuse ratio, throughput, and mean TTFT (a) compute-bound / high density; (b) compute-abundant / low density. Capacity can raise throughput when computation limits service; under arrival-limited service, throughput saturates near request arrivals. Prefetch timeline Tier results Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.3, Figure 5, p. 5. B04

Backup B5 — Full Tier Reuse Results Four panels: DRAM and disk under Trace A at two instance scales High-density 1-instance workloads have longer prefetch windows. Four-instance workloads are compute-abundant, with shorter queue times. Main density evidence Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.3, Figure 6, p. 6. B05

Backup B6 — Planner, Simulator, and Selector Kareto replays recent traces to plan the following service period Planner generates configurations; simulator estimates their outcomes; Pareto selector returns non-dominated choices for the online system. Group TTL method Pareto search Source: Kareto v1, Section 4.1, Figure 9. B06

Backup B7 — Kareto Simulator Architecture Figure 4 shows the original components and modeled data flow The paper describes a discrete-event inference engine, empirical attention/FFN execution times, radix-tree shared prefix reuse, and hierarchical layer-wise KV prefetching. Simulator overview Profiling Source: Kareto v1, Section 3.2, Figure 4, p. 4. B07

Backup B8 — Adaptive Pareto Search Ablation Fewer simulated points with comparable reported hypervolume Grid search: DRAM 0–4096 GB in 256 GB steps; disk 0–3600 GB in 120 GB steps. Adaptive search starts coarser, then refines. Hypervolume uses the same dominated reference point for the comparison. Search method Source: Kareto v1, Sections 4.2 and 5.3.1, Algorithm 1 and Figure 13. B08

Backup B9 — Prefix-Tree Reuse Concentration A few subtrees account for most reuse events Ranking motivates giving frequently reused prefix groups individual retention policies. Reuse intervals ROI allocation Group TTL overview Source: Kareto v1, Section 4.3, Figure 10. B09

Backup B10 — Group Reuse-Interval Distributions Top subtrees have distinct reuse intervals across early and late trace windows Group-specific TTLs reflect differences among subtree reuse patterns. Group TTL overview Source: Kareto v1, Section 4.3, Figure 11. B10

Backup B11 — ROI-Aware Group TTL Allocation Prefix groups receive different TTLs under a shared storage budget ROIg(t) = Hg(t) Cg(t) , max t X g Hg(tg) s.t. X g Cg(tg) ≤B Hg(t) counts hits for group g under TTL t. Cg(t) measures its capacity-time consumption. First find each group’s ROI-efficient TTL, scale to the shared budget, then refine by constrained optimization. The paper uses SLSQP with multiple starts. ROI is hits per capacity-time, not financial profit or energy saved. Group TTL affects disk retention. Group TTL overview Source: Kareto v1, Section 4.3, Algorithm 2. B11

Backup B12 — Group TTL Reuse Ablation Reuse-ratio and end-to-end benefits vary across workloads and scales Group TTL improves reuse most clearly for Trace B/C in reported settings; gains can be marginal for Trace A or 4 instances. Main findings Source: Kareto v1, Section 5.3.2, Figure 14. B12

Backup B13 — Group TTL Reuse-Interval Ablation TTL-specific storage retention responds to group reuse intervals Read together with Figure 14’s reuse-ratio comparison and Figure 16’s end-to-end metrics; this panel reports study conditions, not a single universal effect. Main findings Source: Kareto v1, Section 5.3.2, Figure 15. B13

Backup B14 — Group TTL Performance and Cost Objective metrics compare group TTL with fixed TTL across traces The paper reports benefits especially for Trace B/C; effects depend on workload, disk budget, DRAM capacity, and instance count. No additional percentages are inferred here. Main findings Source: Kareto v1, Section 5.3.2, Figure 16. Figure 18 appears in HTML source for Trace C panels. B14

Backup B15 — Real-System Simulator Validation Real and simulated responses across request rates and storage tiers Tested configurations: GPU-only, GPU + host DRAM, GPU + disk. Maximum deviations: mean TTFT 19.2%, total throughput 6.5%, hit rate 2.0%. These data do not validate energy or carbon estimates. Validation summary Source: Kareto v1, Section 5.4. Versioned arXiv HTML labels this Figure 19; supplied figure filename is Fig17. B15

Backup B16 — KV Reuse Energy Break-Even Model Proposed analytical comparison, not a Kareto result Eretain = Eoffload + Eretention(t) + pErestore Ediscard = pErecompute Retain KV offload + stor- age + restore Discard KV future recomputation compare energy Potentially energy-efficient if Eretain < Ediscard. Assumptions: one possible future reuse; p is reuse probability. Shared batch energy, overlapping work, opportunity cost, and physical idle power need additional modeling. Allocated retention cost is not necessarily avoidable idle energy. Research directions GPU energy model Proposed analytical model: not an evaluated result. B16

Backup B17 — Energy and Carbon Accounting Boundaries Keep energy, carbon, and lifecycle allocation boundaries explicit Operational energy / carbon GPU board, CPU, host DRAM, SSD, transfers, server baseline, shared batches, and overlapping prefetch / I/O. EIT = R PIT(t)dt Cop = P t E kWh IT,t PUEt CIt Embodied carbon / safeguards Allocate lifecycle emissions over a declared service boundary. Avoid GPU/HBM double count; count shared batch work once; apply PUE once. Cache eviction does not undo manufacturing emissions. Lower occupancy need not lower physical idle draw. At fixed CI and PUE, energy and operational carbon rank configurations identically. Prior work Energy modeling Proposed accounting method informed by GreenCache, Sections 2.3 and 3.2. B17

Revised Research Scope Focus on single-server and single-rack serving before larger deployments. Earlier scope Cross-data-center routing; WAN; HBM/HBF architecture exploration. Server A: het- erogeneous GPUs + HBM Server B: het- erogeneous GPUs + HBM CPU + DRAM + NVMe + NIC CPU + DRAM + NVMe + NIC Rack switch Revised scope Multi-GPU server and multi-server rack; heterogeneous compute/HBM/bandwidth/power; HBM–DRAM–SSD hierarchy; chat, RAG, long-context, agentic workloads. Intra-server PCIe/NVLink where supported; rack Ethernet/InfiniBand/RDMA where deployed. WAN out of scope. NIC = network interface card; RDMA = remote direct memory access. Model placement and scheduling methods follow gap validation. Research Discussion 1 / 10

Power, Energy, and Carbon Metrics Optimize system energy under SLOs; retain full power and carbon accounting. Power (W) Idle / baseline; dynamic / active; average; peak. Static power is not automatically measured idle power. Energy (J, kWh) EIT = R PIT (t)dt Operational energy; J/request; J/output token; J/completed task. Carbon Operational: P t EIT (t) PUE(t) CI(t). Embodied carbon tracked separately over lifecycle. CI in gCO2e/kWh when energy is kWh. Performance and power constraints TTFT, TPOT, SLO attainment, goodput, rack power budget. At fixed CI and PUE, operational-carbon and energy rankings are identical. Embodied carbon is a lifecycle assessment, not runtime energy. Research Discussion 2 / 10

Topic A: Workload-Aware Energy Optimization of Multi-Tier KV Cache Question: Can energy-aware cache choices reduce energy under latency SLOs? HBM DRAM NVMe SSD keep / demote / restore restore / evict Variables Capacity; prefix length; reuse probability/distance; request density; storage I/O; shared batch energy. Research tests Does detailed energy change rankings? When is restore cheaper than recompute? Can policy save energy within SLO? Feasibility Start single server. Verify SSD timing and profile needs first; expand to shared rack KV only if needed. SSD is not assumed to serve each active decode access. Potential contributions: calibrated model, break-even characterization, SLO-constrained policy (all to validate). Research Discussion 4 / 10

Topic B: Energy-Efficient Workload Scheduling on Heterogeneous GPU Racks Question: Does KV locality and marginal batch energy improve GPU choice under SLOs? Incoming workloads Request routing candidate decisions GPU A compute / HBM profile GPU B band- width / power profile GPU C capacity / power profile Validate prior work DynamoLLM and FREESH already study energy-aware scheduling. Check their KV locality, shared-batch, host/storage, and communication models. Initial boundary Start with fixed model/precision, existing replicas, and request routing. Defer heterogeneous TP/PP, layer placement, and phase disaggregation. Research Discussion 5 / 10

Topic C: Energy-Aware KV Cache Management for Agentic LLM Serving Question: Retain, move, or discard inactive session KV for later reuse? Model call 1 Tool execu- tion / wait Model call 2 Tool wait Model call 3 session KV may persist across calls Motivation Multi-turn calls, growing context, long residency, tool waits, session reuse. Potential evidence Session energy; retention/offload behavior; energy per completed task. Verify public traces and tool timing. Separate inference energy from whole-agent energy and assess task quality. Session-aware retention is not new. Topic C may be a workload within Topic A. Research Discussion 6 / 10

Research Gap Validation Plan Measure energy-related gaps before designing a new scheduling method. 1. Workload characterization Chat / RAG / agentic; input/output lengths; KV reuse; working set; session life and idle intervals. 2. Model fidelity Compare LLMServingSim power estimates and calibrated batch/storage/communication extensions against hardware measurements. 3. Ranking comparison HBM only; HBM+DRAM; HBM+DRAM+SSD; recompute vs restore; performance-, cost-, and energy-oriented choices. Core test Does a more accurate system energy model change the ranking of feasible configurations or policies? Hold workload, hardware, policy, completed volume/observation horizon, and SLO constraints constant; vary the energy model. Any ranking reversal shown later must be labeled hypothetical. No outcomes are assumed. Research Discussion 7 / 10

Why LLMServingSim 2.0? A comprehensive, extensible foundation for heterogeneous serving research. Workloads and request simulation Serving runtime and continuous batching Heterogeneous accelera- tors / model parallelism KV cache, memory tiers, communication backend Component power model (documented capabilities) Verified foundation Heterogeneous profiles; serving and network simulation; KV/memory features; documented node-level power fields. Check version specifics Public docs and repo evolve. Audit pinned source, model coverage, component calibration, and feature flags before experiment design. Still to verify Storage idle-power field does not prove SSD cache timing, migration, or I/O contention. Conceptual abstraction of framework; features vary by version. Paper: arXiv:2602.23036. Research Discussion 8 / 10

Proposed Power and Carbon Extensions Integrate calibrated component models into the existing simulation loop. Workload, hardware, tiers, CI/PUE, lifecycle data LLMServingSim serving + mem- ory + commu- nication events Latency, goodput, power, energy, carbon Power extension GPU batch/phase; CPU; DRAM; SSD; links Carbon extension operational + lifecycle embodied Reuse model sources Carbon–SLO batch energy; DRAMPower / storage literature; GreenCache, EcoServe, ACT carbon methods; Kareto tier behavior. Accounting safeguards Avoid adding request energy to shared batch energy; do not double-count GPU/HBM/base; apply PUE once; treat embodied carbon as lifecycle allocation, not runtime-avoided emissions. Region-specific CI is a scenario input, not cross-data-center routing. Calibrate every refined model. Research Discussion 9 / 10

Proposed Next Steps Establish the evaluation framework before choosing an optimization method. Phase 1 – Survey Review power/carbon models; identify code, data, profiling sets; audit LLMServingSim 2.0. Phase 2 – Extend Reproduce baseline; extend energy accounting; add operational and embodied carbon; implement storage behavior only if audit finds gaps. Phase 3 – Calibrate Validate against available measurements; characterize workloads and GPU/storage settings; compare energy and performance choices. Phase 4 – Select topic Validate gaps; choose a feasible research question; then design the necessary method. Discussion Is Topic A the right starting point? Single server or multi-server first? Which traces and hardware are available? Which model extensions are essential? Research Discussion 10 / 10
